prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock and its realisation at the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks (B041) with Katori and Ye as my single-part position. Having read the full exchange, I still think it passes the three tests that matter most to me: the achievement is specific, it is mature, and the credit is clean. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removed the conflict between trapping many atoms for long interrogation and perturbing the clock transition. The Ye group then showed, through careful control of blackbody, collisional and higher-order light shifts, that the idea delivers fractional uncertainty near 1e-18, about two orders of magnitude beyond caesium. Several independent laboratories now reproduce this performance and clocks are compared across continents, so recognition rests on demonstrated results and does not depend on waiting for the formal redefinition of the second. Lindroth's point that the accuracy comes from understood and suppressed systematic shifts is the right emphasis for the citation: this is physics of what can be measured and how accurately, and not only engineering. On the overlap question the chair put to us, I now come down firmly on distinctness: the 2005 prize honoured the frequency comb as a way of counting optical cycles and the 2012 prize honoured control of individual quantum systems, whereas the lattice clock is a new type of atomic reference built on a different principle, and I worry that I stated the overlap concern in round 1 more strongly than the science supports. I read the exchange as showing that B046 and B041 are close, and I do not regard the choice as lopsided.
statement.case_against: The strongest case against B041 is that it may be read as a refinement of the metrological line already recognised in 2005 and 2012, and that its reach into new physics (varying constants, relativistic geodesy, dark-matter searches) is still largely prospective. The second has not been redefined. The two-name credit also leaves out the strontium, ytterbium and ion-clock groups in Paris, Braunschweig and Boulder that contributed to the accuracy record, and I cannot dismiss that. Against B046, I accept that it has the broadest opening support, a clean prediction-then-discovery chain, and that it opened a new class of materials, which is a different kind of impact from a better measurement. The reasons I still do not move are timing and credit: the 2018 discovery is eight years old, the pairing mechanism is unresolved, and the experimental half of the three-name credit omits Yuan Cao and the parallel Dean, Yacoby and Young results, which makes the citation harder to defend than the clock citation.

responses.point: You moved B046 to first place as the cleanest prediction-then-discovery chain, and argued that an open pairing mechanism is no reason to wait because the prize would honour the flat bands and the observed phases.
responses.response: Your argument on the mechanism is fair, and it is the one that has moved me most: the phases are reproduced across groups, so I do not treat the unsettled pairing as disqualifying in principle. In round 1 I also leaned on novelty of principle, but I now think that argument was too coarse. The lattice clock is a new reference system, not a further turn of the comb, and I would not call it a refinement merely because it is metrology. Where we still differ is on credit. You propose that the citation should say the discovery was made by the Jarillo-Herrero group. That is honest, but it asks the citation to carry an attribution the three names do not make, and I see no equivalent problem in the Katori and Ye split. Given the same evidence about maturity, I weight a settled two-name attribution more heavily than you do.

responses.point: You hold that B046 is the best-supported candidate: theory confirmed by a decisive experiment, a field that grew enormously, and eight years being enough because the phases are secure.
responses.response: I agree that the phases are secure and that the theory-plus-experiment pattern is clean, and I have kept B046 as my first alternative for that reason. I would still separate the discovery from the field it spawned. The prize would honour the 2018 observation, and for that observation the experimental credit is the weak point you yourself concede, with Cao as first author and parallel results from Dean, Yacoby and Young. You say the senior-investigator convention gives a defensible trio. I accept it is defensible but not as free of cost as the clock credit. On your side of the exchange I would also add that your own rank of B041 as fifth, with the overlap worry, is the point I have just retracted: the comb counts optical cycles, and the lattice clock supplies a new atomic reference.

responses.point: You called B041 the strongest competing case but weigh B046 higher because it exposed new physics rather than a better measurement of known physics, and you want the citation to rest only on what independent groups have reproduced.
responses.response: I agree with the discipline of citing only reproduced results, and I would apply it to both ballots. For B041 that is easy: independent clocks in several laboratories agree at the 1e-18 level. On the distinction between new physics and better measurement, I accept it as a real difference of kind, but I do not think the lattice clock is merely better measurement of known physics. Magic-wavelength trapping is a new physical mechanism for cancelling a perturbation, and controlling the many-body and blackbody shifts at this level is a new regime of atomic physics. I also grant, as you do, that metrological reach into new physics is still partly promise, and I would not claim otherwise in the citation.

responses.point: You asked that the citation make the atomic-structure control of systematic shifts explicit and that we state plainly why the comb prize does not overlap with the lattice clock.
responses.response: I accept both points and have changed my citation accordingly: it now names the invention of the lattice clock and its realisation at the 1e-18 level, since the accuracy is a consequence of understood shifts. I would also write into the committee's rationale that the comb counts optical cycles and the lattice clock provides the new reference, so overlap is not left to assumption. On the shared alternatives, I am not persuaded that the other lattice, ion and Paris and Braunschweig groups should be added, because a three-name limit and the invention-plus-record credit make Katori and Ye the only workable pair.

responses.point: As chair you moved from B033 to B041 on the grounds of cleanest attribution, independent reproduction and concrete reach into tests of relativity and dark-matter models.
responses.response: I agree with your reading of attribution and reproduction, but I would be careful with the breadth of reach: relativistic geodesy and dark-matter and constant-variation searches are real applications and still mostly prospective, so I would keep them out of the citation and rest on the invention and the accuracy. If the committee does weigh metrology on its demonstrated record, B041 stands without them.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, as I now believe, or as a continuation.
Whether recognition should wait for the formal redefinition of the second; I think not, but I cannot show colleagues will agree.
Whether the omission of other lattice and ion-clock groups can be defended with a two-name credit.
Whether B046 at about eight years, with Cao and the parallel groups outside the credit, would be preferred by colleagues who weight breadth of a new field over precision.
Priority details for the early magic-wavelength proposal and the first lattice-clock demonstrations are from memory and unverified in this stage.
statement.conflict_note: I spent a research stay in John Hall's laboratory, and Jun Ye is a close scientific descendant of that JILA environment, so I disclose this connection for B041. It is a documented professional link to a mentor and not a collaboration with Ye or Katori, and I know of no joint work, funding or institutional tie to either. I also note proximity to the trapped-ion and cold-atom community (B018, B038) without a specific relationship to Cirac, Zoller or Blatt. The chair has asked whether this requires recusal. I think disclosure is sufficient, and I will accept the committee's decision, including recusal from the B041 vote, if colleagues judge the Hall link too close. I have no tie to any B046 name.
